## Required Library
```r
# nls() is in base R (stats), loaded by default — no package installation needed
```

## Syntax

```r
nls(formula, data = df, start = list(param1 = value1, param2 = value2))
```
::: {.desc-item}
`nls()` fits non-linear models by estimating parameter values that best match the data.
Unlike `lm()`, you write the full model equation directly in the formula.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why use `nls()`?
Use `nls()` when your data follows a curved relationship that a straight line cannot describe well.
Typical examples in pharmacy include dose-response curves (e.g., sigmoidal Emax models), dissolution profiles (e.g., Weibull models), and saturation/enzyme kinetics (e.g., Michaelis-Menten).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Start values are required
`nls()` needs reasonable starting guesses in `start = list(...)`.
They do not need to be exact, but should be in the right range.
:::

## Model Used In These Examples

For simplicity, the examples below use a 3-parameter sigmoidal model with fixed slope (`Hill = 1`):

$$
y = \text{Bottom} + \frac{\text{Top} - \text{Bottom}}{1 + (\text{EC}_{50}/x)}
$$

`Bottom` and `Top` are the lower and upper plateaus, and `EC50` is the concentration where response is halfway between them.

## Examples

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Fit a simple dose-response curve</summary>
<div class="example-body">

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dose_response <- tibble(
  dose_uM = c(0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  response_pct = c(2, 6, 14, 35, 63, 86, 96)
)

fit_sigmoid <- nls(
  # 3-parameter sigmoid with fixed slope (Hill = 1)
  response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM)),
  data = dose_response,
  # Start guesses: low plateau, high plateau, midpoint concentration
  start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
)

coef(fit_sigmoid)
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Extract EC50 from the fitted model</summary>
<div class="example-body">

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dose_response <- tibble(
  dose_uM = c(0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  response_pct = c(2, 6, 14, 35, 63, 86, 96)
)

fit_sigmoid <- nls(
  # Same model as above
  response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM)),
  data = dose_response,
  start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
)

ec50 <- coef(fit_sigmoid)[["EC50"]]
cat("EC50:", signif(ec50, 3), "uM\n")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Predict and plot the fitted non-linear curve</summary>
<div class="example-body">
The points are your measured data.
The line is built from many model predictions across a fine x-grid, then added with `geom_line()`.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dose_response <- tibble(
  dose_uM = c(0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  response_pct = c(2, 6, 14, 35, 63, 86, 96)
)

fit_sigmoid <- nls(
  response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM)),
  data = dose_response,
  start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
)

curve_data <- tibble(
  # Creates a fine grid of x-values for plotting the fitted curve
  dose_uM = seq(0.1, 100, length.out = 500)) %>%
  # Predict y-values from fitted model for each x in the grid
  mutate(pred_response_pct = predict(fit_sigmoid, newdata = .))

ggplot(dose_response, aes(x = dose_uM, y = response_pct)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(y = pred_response_pct), linewidth = 1, colour = "#3C5E3E") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Dose-Response Curve Fitted with nls()",
    x = "Dose (uM)",
    y = "Response (%)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```
</div>
</details>

</div>

## Evaluating Model Fit

Fitting a curve is only useful if it actually describes the data well. A few diagnostics help you judge that.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What to check
- **Residual standard error** — how far, on average, the observed values fall from the fitted curve (smaller is better, in the units of your response).
- **Parameter estimates and standard errors** — from `summary()`; large standard errors relative to the estimate suggest the parameter is poorly identified by your data.
- **Residual plot** — residuals should scatter randomly around zero with no obvious curve or trend. A pattern means the model shape may be wrong.
- **Convergence** — `nls()` should finish without a "singular gradient" or "convergence failure" error; if it does, your start values may need adjusting.
:::

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Check the model summary</summary>
<div class="example-body">
`summary()` reports parameter estimates, standard errors, and the residual standard error.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dose_response <- tibble(
  dose_uM = c(0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  response_pct = c(2, 6, 14, 35, 63, 86, 96)
)

fit_sigmoid <- nls(
  response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM)),
  data = dose_response,
  start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
)

summary(fit_sigmoid)
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary>Plot residuals to check for patterns</summary>
<div class="example-body">
`residuals()` gives the difference between observed and predicted values for each point.
Random scatter around zero suggests a good fit; a curve or trend suggests the model doesn't match the data's shape.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dose_response <- tibble(
  dose_uM = c(0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  response_pct = c(2, 6, 14, 35, 63, 86, 96)
)

fit_sigmoid <- nls(
  response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM)),
  data = dose_response,
  start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
)

residual_data <- dose_response %>%
  mutate(resid = residuals(fit_sigmoid))

ggplot(residual_data, aes(x = dose_uM, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals from Sigmoid Fit",
    x = "Dose (uM)",
    y = "Residual (Observed - Predicted)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```
</div>
</details>

</div>

## Argument Overview
<p class="arg-intro">Required arguments must be included when using a function while optional arguments can be included on demand.</p>

::: {.arg-section}
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>formula</code> — non-linear model equation <span class="arg-types">formula</span> <span class="arg-badge required">Required</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
Defines the model you want to fit.
Write the response on the left and the full non-linear expression on the right.

```r
response_pct ~ Bottom + (Top - Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / dose_uM))
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> <code>formula</code></p>
</div>
</details>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>data</code> — data frame with model variables <span class="arg-types">data frame | tibble</span> <span class="arg-badge optional">Optional</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
Data source used to evaluate the variables in the formula.

```r
nls(formula = ..., data = dose_response, start = ...)
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> <code>data.frame</code> | <code>tibble</code></p>
</div>
</details>

<details class="arg-item">
<summary><code>start</code> — starting values for parameters <span class="arg-types">named list</span> <span class="arg-badge required">Required</span></summary>
<div class="arg-body">
Named list with initial guesses for all unknown parameters.
`nls()` uses these values as the starting point for optimisation.

```r
start = list(Bottom = 0, Top = 100, EC50 = 5)
```

<p class="data-types"><strong>Data Types:</strong> named <code>list</code> of numeric values</p>
</div>
</details>
:::
